en: I have already replied to your message.
tamil: நான் ஏற்கனவே உங்க மெசேஜுக்கு பதில் அனுப்பிட்டேன்.
context: Politely telling someone you have done it.
explain: 'Already' with present perfect shows it is done before now.
usage: Use it when someone follows up and you have already answered.
leelaQ: Did you reply to the client's message?
answer: Yes, I have already replied to it.

en: Have you already asked someone else?
tamil: நீங்க ஏற்கனவே வேற யார்கிட்டயாவது கேட்டீங்களா?
context: Checking what the person already knows.
explain: 'Already' with present perfect checks if something is done before now.
usage: Use it when someone asks you for help and may have tried others first.
leelaQ: Who do you ask first when you have a doubt in your work?
answer: I ask my team lead, and then I ask my friends.

en: It is about ten kilometres from my house.
tamil: அது என் வீட்டுல இருந்து சுமார் பத்து கிலோமீட்டர்.
context: Answering about a distance.
explain: 'About' gives a rough number. In India we say kilometres for distance.
usage: Use it when someone asks how far a place is.
leelaQ: How far is your office from your house?
answer: It is about eight kilometres from my house.

en: Please wait, I will answer in a minute.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் இருங்க, ஒரு நிமிஷத்துல பதில் சொல்றேன்.
context: Asking someone to wait.
explain: 'Please wait' is the request. 'I will answer' is the promise.
usage: Use it when you are busy with another task and someone asks something.
leelaQ: What do you say to a person when you are busy?
answer: Please wait, I will answer in a minute.

en: I would say it is a good place for families.
tamil: குடும்பங்களுக்கு இது நல்ல இடம்னு நான் சொல்வேன்.
context: Giving your opinion about a place.
explain: 'I would say' makes your opinion sound polite and careful.
usage: Use it when a friend asks for your opinion on a hotel or park.
leelaQ: Is that park good for children?
answer: I would say it is a good place for children.

en: I'm afraid I can't attend the party.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், என்னால பார்ட்டிக்கு வர முடியாது.
context: Refusing an invitation politely.
explain: 'I'm afraid' is a polite way to give bad news or say no.
usage: Use it to refuse an invitation from a boss or friend politely.
leelaQ: Can you come to my birthday party on Saturday?
answer: I'm afraid I can't, I have a family function.

en: I have a bad headache, so I am leaving early today.
tamil: எனக்கு தலைவலி, அதனால சீக்கிரம் வீட்டுக்குப் போறேன்.
context: Giving a reason to a colleague.
explain: 'So' shows the result. 'Going home' is a plan for the near future.
usage: Use it when your team lead asks why you are leaving early.
leelaQ: Why are you leaving the office early today?
answer: I have a bad headache, so I am going home.

en: Is it all right if I answer in Tamil first?
tamil: நான் முதல்ல தமிழ்ல பதில் சொன்னா பரவாயில்லையா?
context: Asking permission to use your own language.
explain: 'Is it all right if ...?' asks permission politely.
usage: Use it when you cannot find the English words quickly.
leelaQ: What do you do if you cannot find an English word?
answer: I say it in Tamil first, and then I try in English.

en: My birthday is in March, on the twelfth.
tamil: என் பிறந்தநாள் மார்ச் மாசம் பனிரெண்டாம் தேதி.
context: Answering a personal question.
explain: Use 'in' for the month and 'on' for the date.
usage: Use it when someone asks your date of birth in a friendly way.
leelaQ: When is your birthday?
answer: My birthday is on the fifth of June.

en: I believe the shop opens at nine.
tamil: கடை ஒன்பது மணிக்கு திறக்கும்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Giving information you are not completely sure about.
explain: 'I believe' is a little stronger than 'I think' but still not certain.
usage: Use it when a neighbour asks the shop timing and you do not know exactly.
leelaQ: What time does the bakery open?
answer: I believe it opens at seven in the morning.

en: Yes, I am free after lunch.
tamil: ஆமா, சாப்பாட்டுக்கு அப்புறம் நான் ஃப்ரீ.
context: Replying to a request for your time.
explain: 'Free' here means not busy. Add a time to make the answer useful.
usage: Use it when a colleague asks if you are available to talk.
leelaQ: Are you free to meet this afternoon?
answer: Yes, I am free after three o'clock.

en: Do you mean this month or next month?
tamil: நீங்க இந்த மாசத்தை சொல்றீங்களா, அடுத்த மாசத்தையா?
context: Clearing a doubt about time.
explain: 'Do you mean ...?' checks what the other person meant.
usage: Use it when someone asks about a deadline or leave and the month is unclear.
leelaQ: What do you ask if someone's date is not clear?
answer: I ask, do you mean this month or next month?

en: I was born in Salem, but my family moved to Chennai.
tamil: நான் சேலத்துல பிறந்தேன், ஆனா எங்க குடும்பம் சென்னைக்கு மாறிடுச்சு.
context: Giving background about yourself.
explain: Use past tense for both finished events. 'But' adds the change.
usage: Use it when someone asks about your hometown and your background.
leelaQ: Where were you born, and where do you live now?
answer: I was born in Madurai, and I live in Chennai now.

en: Give me your number, and I will call you back.
tamil: உங்க நம்பர் குடுங்க, நான் திரும்ப கூப்பிடுறேன்.
context: Offering to call back.
explain: An imperative joined with 'and I will' gives a request and a promise.
usage: Use it when someone asks something and you want to answer by phone later.
leelaQ: What do you say when you cannot answer on a call now?
answer: Give me your number, and I will call you back.

en: I will probably take the morning train.
tamil: நான் ஒருவேளை காலை ட்ரெயின்ல போவேன்.
context: Answering about your travel plan.
explain: 'Probably' goes between 'will' and the verb.
usage: Use it when a friend asks how you will travel and you have not booked yet.
leelaQ: How will you go to Chennai next week?
answer: I will probably take the night bus.

en: I do not know the answer, but I can ask my teacher.
tamil: எனக்கு பதில் தெரியாது, ஆனா என் டீச்சர்கிட்ட கேட்கலாம்.
context: Being honest when you do not know.
explain: It is fine to say you do not know. Then offer to find the answer.
usage: Use it in class or at work when you do not know and want to help.
leelaQ: Do you know the answer to this question?
answer: I do not know, but I can look it up.

en: I usually cook at home on weekdays.
tamil: நான் பொதுவா வாரநாட்கள்ல வீட்டுலயே சமைப்பேன்.
context: Answering about your eating habits.
explain: Put 'usually' before the main verb. 'On weekdays' means Monday to Friday.
usage: Use it when a friend asks if you eat outside often.
leelaQ: Do you eat outside or cook at home?
answer: I usually cook at home, and I eat out on Sundays.

en: Which part is not clear to you?
tamil: எந்தப் பகுதி உங்களுக்கு புரியல?
context: Asking a student or colleague what they did not follow.
explain: 'Which part' helps you find the exact doubt before explaining again.
usage: Use it as a teacher or senior when someone says they did not understand.
leelaQ: What do you ask a friend who did not understand your explanation?
answer: I ask, which part is not clear to you?

en: Yes, my brother works in Singapore.
tamil: ஆமா, என் அண்ணன் சிங்கப்பூர்ல வேலை பார்க்கிறாங்க.
context: Answering about a family member.
explain: Third person singular verbs take s: brother works.
usage: Use it when someone asks if anyone in your family is abroad.
leelaQ: Does anyone in your family live abroad?
answer: Yes, my uncle lives in Dubai.

en: I am studying engineering in my final year.
tamil: நான் இன்ஜினியரிங் கடைசி வருஷம் படிச்சுட்டு இருக்கேன்.
context: Telling about your studies.
explain: 'Final year' is the last year of a course.
usage: Use it when someone asks what you are studying now.
leelaQ: What are you studying now?
answer: I am studying commerce in my second year.

en: I stayed back in the office to finish some work.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் வேலையை முடிக்க நான் ஆபீஸ்ல இருந்தேன்.
context: Explaining why you were late reaching home.
explain: 'Stayed back' is common in Indian English for staying after hours.
usage: Use it when family asks why you came home late.
leelaQ: Why did you come home so late yesterday?
answer: I stayed back in the office to finish a report.

en: Are you free to talk now, or shall I call later?
tamil: நீங்க இப்போ பேசுற அளவுக்கு ஃப்ரீயா, இல்ல நான் அப்புறம் கூப்பிடவா?
context: Checking on a phone call.
explain: 'Shall I' is a polite offer. Two options keep the question easy.
usage: Use it when you call someone who may be busy.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you call someone who may be busy?
answer: I ask, are you free to talk now?

en: In my opinion, the first option is better.
tamil: என் கருத்துப்படி, முதல் ஆப்ஷன் நல்லது.
context: Giving your opinion in a discussion.
explain: 'In my opinion' starts a clear and polite opinion.
usage: Use it in a team discussion when asked to choose one option.
leelaQ: Which option do you like more, the first or the second?
answer: In my opinion, the second option is better.

en: Please explain your question once again.
tamil: தயவு செஞ்சு உங்க கேள்வியை இன்னொரு தடவை விளக்குங்க.
context: Asking for an explanation of an unclear question.
explain: 'Explain' asks for more detail, not only repeating.
usage: Use it when a question is long or confusing.
leelaQ: What do you say if a question is confusing?
answer: I say, please explain your question once again.

en: I know him very well, we studied together.
tamil: எனக்கு அவனை நல்லா தெரியும், நாங்க சேர்ந்து படிச்சோம்.
context: Answering if you know a person.
explain: 'Know' is not used in the continuous form. 'Studied together' gives the reason.
usage: Use it when someone asks if you know a friend of a friend.
leelaQ: Do you know Karthik from your college?
answer: Yes, I know him well, we were classmates.
